title: Sell Mineral Rights in De Beque, CO

metaTitle: Sell Mineral Rights in De Beque, CO | Piceance Gas
metaDescription: Own minerals near De Beque, Mesa County? We buy Piceance Basin gas interests, price against recent royalty checks, and close on your timeline.
heroLead: De Beque sits on the eastern lip of the Piceance Basin, where Mancos and Williams Fork gas has been produced off and on for four decades.
intro: Mesa County mineral ownership around De Beque is usually a leftover piece of a bigger ranch parcel, split off when a family sold the surface but kept the minerals, or when a well was drilled and the estate got carved between heirs. We buy these interests directly and price them against what the acreage has actually paid, not what a leasing company quoted a decade ago.

Piceance gas is a boom-bust story locally: heavy activity in the mid-2000s, a long lull as gas prices sat flat, and periodic re-permitting near Rulison and Parachute that ripples west toward De Beque. If your interest has been quiet for years, that is normal for this part of the basin, not a sign the minerals are worthless.

sections.heading: What we look at first
paragraphs: We start with the same documents a title examiner would want: your deed, any lease of record with the Mesa County Clerk and Recorder, and, if the tract has ever produced, the operator's division order and check stubs. Those stubs tell us more about current value than any online estimator, because they show actual net revenue interest and how fast a well's output is declining.

sections.heading: Producing versus non-producing acreage
paragraphs: A De Beque interest tied to an active Williams Fork well prices differently than raw, unleased minerals with no drilling history. Producing tracts get valued off a decline curve applied to trailing production; non-producing acreage gets valued more on comparable regional lease and sale activity, since there is no revenue stream yet to underwrite against.

sections.heading: Split estate and access
paragraphs: Most of this ground is split estate, meaning someone else may own the surface while you hold the minerals below it. That does not change your right to a lease or a sale, but it does affect how an operator negotiates surface use agreements, which in turn affects timing. We factor typical Piceance surface-access friction into how we underwrite a De Beque offer.

faqs.question: Is my De Beque interest still worth something if the well has slowed down?
faqs.answer: Usually yes, though a declined well prices lower than a fresh one. We run the numbers off your actual check history rather than assuming a flat rate.

faqs.question: Do you need my lease before you can make an offer?
faqs.answer: It helps but is not required. We can pull recorded lease and unit information from the Mesa County Clerk and Recorder's office if you cannot locate your own copy.

faqs.question: How fast can a sale close once we agree on price?
faqs.answer: Most De Beque transactions close within two to four weeks, mainly limited by how long it takes to confirm title with the county.

faqs.question: What if my interest has never produced?
faqs.answer: We can still make an offer based on comparable Piceance lease and sale activity in Mesa County, priced lower than producing acreage since there is no revenue history yet.
